newsitem.title: IVORY COAST: FOCUS - Donors still see Ivory Coast-IMF deal soon.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Donors still see Ivory Coast-IMF deal soon.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund and Ivory Coast failed to agree on a new structural adjustment programme at talks here last week, but donor sources said a deal was still more than likely by the end of October.
The Ivorian government had been confident of a deal, which the country needs to set in train a series of linked debt reduction programmes.

A donor source said a deal was now "extremely unlikely" to be ready to put before the next IMF board meeting in September, but analysts said one might be concluded later that month at the annual IMF and World Bank meetings in Hong Kong.

Asked what the sticking points were, a second donor source mentioned "the shape of the budget over the next two years" but he added that it was "nothing dramatic, just a mixed bag of micro-management things."
He said technical work would continue through August and September and he was confident that agreement could be reached by the end of October.

Analysts were reassured that Ivory Coast had agreed to commodity reforms, including the complete reform of the Caistab commodities marketing board, seen as a potential stumbling block since the government had resisted it for so long.
"I was a bit worried that the Caistab was going to hamstring the whole deal. Frankly, I'm surprised that anything else was able to stop a deal," said one London-based analyst.
He was confident there would be an agreement soon.
"The IMF and World Bank consider Ivory Coast as one of their pet projects," he said.

They agreed extensive loans after the 50 percent devaluation of the CFA franc in 1994, and economic results since have been impressive, with seven percent growth in both 1995 and 1996 and inflation kept under control.
Similar confidence was expressed by another bank analyst.

"If the problem had been over the Caistab, I would have been worried, but it looks like the big issues have been sorted out," he said, describing even issues such as poverty reduction as "wrapping paper" by comparison.

Ivory Coast, the world's biggest producer of cocoa, has agreed to reform the role of the Caistab, freeing marketing prices and leaving the private sector to take charge of export auctions for coffee and cocoa from 1999 at the latest.

The prices paid to peasant farmers are likely to go up as a result of the reforms, going some way to alleviating rural poverty in Ivory Coast, one of the donors' main concerns along with a lack of transparency in the state budget.

Securing an IMF Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) is vital if Ivory Coast is to get a further rescheduling of its official debt owed to governments in the Paris Club, and for its hopes of securing a wider debt write-off under the donor community's Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative.
One donor source suggested that the talks were taking longer than necessary because of the technical detail required for the "ambitious" HIPC deal, coordinated by the IMF and World Bank.
An IMF deal is also needed to secure from donors the "up-front" money to implement a reduction deal with commercial banks signed after years of tough negotiations in May.
